newsitem.title: POLAND: Candidate states content with EU summit deal.
newsitem.headline: Candidate states content with EU summit deal.

text.p: East European states bent on joining the EU said the limited deal reached by its members in Amsterdam on Wednesday would allow enlargement to go forward, but some voiced concern over maintaining the pace.
The Amsterdam summit was supposed to resolve issues facing the 15 EU members so they could begin accession talks with a first group of future entrants in six months' time.
The updated treaty that was finally agreed left various questions undecided, but Central and East European officials said this was unlikely to be a major problem.
"The most important thing is that the results and shortcomings of the summit will not slow down the start of the enlargement," Hungarian Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs said.
"Accession talks would start as originally planned, six months after the inter-governmental conference," he added.

Warsaw's Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati was less optimistic. He said Poland still counted on starting talks as agreed in January, but signals from Brussels suggested they could be delayed to April or May.

"Signals are flowing from Brussels 'Oh don't be so sure that it will be exactly January, it could be April'," he told a Polish business group meeting in Warsaw late on Tuesday as the outcome of the Amsterdam meeting was becoming clear.
"This is not a dramatic difference in time and we are not especially uneasy, although from a political viewpoint it would be better to start talks in January as was planned," he said.
Candidate countries were not especially worried that the summit put off final decisions on key issues such as changing the balance of power in the bloc and on its defence structure.
Rosati, who hopes Poland will join by 2001 or 2002 but views the start of talks as crucial, even saw a bright side.
"Maybe it is better...because that means they can be decided with our participation, if we manage to join the EU in four or five years' time," said Rosati.

Regional officials said the main thing was for the EU to give its "avis" opinion on candidates' readiness as planned on July 16, then for a December EU meeting in Luxembourg to decide when talks with the first group would start.
Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Lithuania, Latvia, Bulgaria and Romania have applied for EU membership. Cyprus also hopes to join.
Which will be in the first group is yet to be decided.
Slovenia, for example, hopes to be included but must first change its constitution to allow foreigners to buy land so its association agreement with the EU can be ratified.

"Although the ambitions of the Amsterdam summit were bigger than the results, we believe these are sufficient for the process of EU enlargement to continue according to plan," said Marija Adanja, consultant at Slovenia's foreign ministry.
European parliamentarian Herbert Boesch said in Bratislava that Slovakia would have to prove itself ready.
"The train (to EU enlargement) is already moving and we have stressed that it depends on Slovakia alone if it is to be able to catch up with it," Boesch told a news conference.
Candidate states including Poland, which expects criticism of its readiness and economic reforms in the EU's July avis, already know that once talks start they are likely to be tough.
For some analysts, the difficulty in reaching the summit deal was an ominous sign for agreement on enlargement.

"Explicitly, there is no change vis-a-vis enlargement, but implicitly the very proceedings of the summit indicate it is going to be more difficult than we expected," said Jiri Sedivy, deputy head of the Prague Institute of International Relations.
Sedivy said it was unlikely that the Czech Republic or any other leading contenders -- which also include Poland and Hungary -- would be admitted before 2005.
